theme: Jerusalem’s mourning; the city as widow
readingInstruction: Read Lamentations 1:1-2:22. The book of Lamentations is a collection of five poems of grief over the fall of Jerusalem. Read it slowly and honestly, without hurrying to the good news. Notice who is speaking in each part.
settingTheScene: Lamentations was traditionally written by Jeremiah, though the text does not name an author. It follows the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and the five poems are written as acrostics: the first four use the Hebrew alphabet as a frame, a way of giving order to disorder. The book shows how to grieve in faith. It does not offer quick answers. It gives words for sorrow so that the people can bring it to God.
observation: “How lonely sits the city that was full of people! How like a widow has she become” (1:1).
“She weeps bitterly in the night, with tears on her cheeks; among all her lovers she has none to comfort her” (1:2).
“The LORD has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions” (1:5).
“Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (1:12).
“The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word” (1:18).
“The Lord has become like an enemy; he has swallowed up Israel” (2:5).
“My eyes are spent with weeping; my stomach churns; my bile is poured out to the ground” (2:11).
“Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the night watches! Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord!” (2:19).
interpretation:
The opening line is among the saddest in the Bible. “How lonely sits the city that was full of people!” Jerusalem is pictured as a widow, once great among the nations and now a slave. She weeps in the night. Her friends have betrayed her. Her roads mourn because no one comes to the festivals. Her priests groan, her young women grieve. And no one comforts her.

The poem speaks in two voices: the narrator, who looks at the city and describes her pain, and Jerusalem herself, who speaks from verse 9 on. “Look, O LORD, and see, for I am despised.” The most piercing cry is in verse 12: “Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by?” It is the cry of someone suffering whose pain is invisible to the busy.

Yet already in chapter 1 there is honesty about the cause. “The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word.” The poet does not blame God for injustice. He confesses, and still he cries for help. Grief and repentance go together.

Chapter 2 is more shocking. The speaker says that the Lord himself has become like an enemy. The language is of God’s anger: he has torn down the stronghold, rejected his altar, and scorned his sanctuary. This was the hardest thing for the exiles to accept: God had done this. Yet the point of the poem is that God is real and his word is true.

The turning point is verse 19: “Arise, cry out in the night… pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord!” The right response to sorrow is to bring it to God. Lamentations teaches us that lament is a form of prayer, and that to pour out our hearts to God is itself an act of faith.
connection: Jesus wept over Jerusalem and said, “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Luke 13:34). On the road to Golgotha, he told the women, “Do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves” (Luke 23:28). Romans 12:15 says, “Weep with those who weep.” Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus offered up prayers with loud cries and tears. Matthew 5:4: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.”
application:
Spend time grieving something you have lost, without trying to fix it. Pour it out to God.

Be present with someone who is suffering. Do not hurry them. Sit with them.

Pray with the words of Lamentations 2:19 when you cannot find your own.
prayerPrompts: Pour out your heart to God, naming a sorrow.
Confess where you have rebelled against his word.
Ask him to look on your affliction.
